chunks: Peak current mode below and above 50% duty.
The question: When using peak current mode control, what happens when the duty cycle is less than 50% during noise events/load perturbations?
What about when the duty cycle is greater than 50%?
In a peak current mode buck converter, the switch turns off when the inductor current reaches a set peak.
If noise or a load change makes the current a little wrong in one cycle, that error carries into the next cycle.
There it flips sign and gets scaled by a factor that depends on the duty cycle D (the share of time the switch is on): D over (1-D) .
Below 50% duty that factor is under one, so the error dies out. Above 50% it is over one, so the error grows into an oscillation.
Think of a microphone near its speaker. A small sound comes out louder or quieter each trip around the loop. If each trip makes it quieter, it fades away.
If each trip makes it louder, you get a squeal. Here the "loop" is one switching cycle, and the multiplier is D over (1-D) .
The analogy misses one detail: the error also flips sign every cycle, so it alternates up and down.
The same kick at four operating points. At D equals 0. 4 (green) the starting current converges back to its steady value within about a dozen cycles. At D equals 0.
5 (orange) the error never decays. At D equals 0. 6 (red) the error grows by 1.
5 times per cycle and then locks to a large alternating pattern, which includes cycles with almost no on-time and cycles at full width. The blue dashed curve is D equals 0.
6 with a ramp of half the down-slope: stable.
Duty cycle (D): the fraction of each switching period the main switch is on.
Peak current mode: a control method where the switch turns off when the inductor current hits a target peak.
Disturbance: a small kick to the current, such as a noise spike or a load step.
Subharmonic oscillation: alternating long and short pulses at half the switching frequency ("Subharmonic oscillation explained").
Slope compensation: an added ramp that fixes this problem ("Slope compensation and when it's needed").
Say a disturbance leaves the current 60 milliamps off. At D equals 0. 25 the multiplier is 0. 25 over 0. 75 equals 1 over 3 .
The errors go 60 milliamps, then -20 milliamps, then plus 6. 7 milliamps, and fade out. At D equals 0. 75 the multiplier is 0. 75 over 0. 25 equals 3 .
The errors go 60 milliamps, -180 milliamps, plus 540 milliamps, and keep growing until the converter hits its limits. That is the whole idea.
"In peak current mode a disturbance, like noise tripping the comparator early or a load step, shows up as a current error that flips sign each cycle and is multiplied by D over one minus D.
Below 50 percent that's less than one, so the error dies out and noise only adds a bit of jitter.
Above 50 percent it's greater than one, so the error grows every cycle, giving alternating long and short pulses at half the switching frequency, until the duty limits clamp it.
Slope compensation fixes it."
